extracted.intended_audience: immigration applicants, petitioners, attorneys, stakeholders, and public commenters on DHS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory criteria and procedural requirements for DHS/USCIS determinations of whether an alien is "likely at any time to become a public charge," including definitions of public benefits, household composition, minimum factors to consider, heavily weighed factors, related bond rules, and Paperwork Reduction Act comment guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) comment points for information collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on this information collection should address one or more of the following four points: (1) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (3) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting electronic submission of responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments are encouraged and will be accepted for 60 days from publication; all submissions must include the OMB Control Number in the body of the letter and the agency name; avoid duplicate submissions by using only one method under ADDRESSES/I. Public Participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Public Charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Charge. Public charge means an alien who receives one or more public benefit, as defined in paragraph (b) of this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional trigger for the public charge ground of inadmissibility; subsequent entries define 'public benefit' and how receipt counts toward a public charge finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Public Benefit (monetizable benefits threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public benefit means any of the following monetizable benefits, where the cumulative value of one or more of the listed benefits exceeds 15 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) for a household of one within any period of 12 consecutive months, based on the per-month FPG for the months during which the benefits are received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetizable benefits counted toward this 15% FPG threshold include specified cash assistance programs (see next entry) and non-cash benefits monetized under 8 CFR 212.24; the 12-month rolling period and per-month FPG calculation determine whether the threshold is exceeded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizable benefits included (cash assistance)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) Any Federal, State, local, or tribal cash assistance for income maintenance, including: (A) Supplemental Security Income (SSI), 42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq.; (B) Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), 42 U.S.C. 601 et seq.; or (C) Federal, State or local cash benefit programs for income maintenance (often called “General Assistance” in the State context, but which may exist under other names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These cash programs are explicitly listed as monetizable benefits; receipt of such programs contributes to the 15% FPG monetizable-benefit threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetized non-cash benefits counted toward monetizable threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: (ii) Non-cash benefits, monetized as set forth in 8 CFR 212.24: (A) Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP); (B) Section 8 Housing Assistance under the Housing Choice Voucher Program; (C) Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance (including Moderate Rehabilitation) and related programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified non-cash benefits are monetized per 8 CFR 212.24 and contribute to the 15% FPG test when their cumulative monetized value exceeds the threshold within a 12-month period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-monetizable benefits (time-based counting rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any of one or more of the following non-monetizable benefits if received for more than 12 months in the aggregate within a 36 month period (such that, for instance, receipt of two non-monetizable benefits in one month counts as two months): (i) Medicaid (with enumerated exceptions); (ii) Any benefit provided for institutionalization for long-term care at government expense; (iii) Premium and Cost Sharing Subsidies for Medicare Part D; (iv) Subsidized Housing under the Housing Act of 1937.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-monetizable benefits do not use the 15% monetization test but instead trigger consideration if the cumulative count of months (counting multiple concurrent benefits as multiple months) exceeds 12 months within a 36-month lookback period; Medicaid has specified exceptions (emergency medical, IDEA-funded services, school-based benefits for eligible children, certain children of U.S. citizens in adoption/citizenship contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination receipt rule (monetizable + non-monetizable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The receipt of a combination of monetizable benefits where the cumulative value of such benefits is equal to or less than 15 percent of the Federal Poverty Guidelines for a household size of one within any period of 12 consecutive [months], together with one or more non-monetizable benefits if such non-monetizable benefits are received for more than 9 months in the aggregate within a 36 month period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combined lower-level monetizable receipt (<=15% FPG) plus more than 9 aggregate months of non-monetizable benefits within 36 months can together count toward public benefit receipt for public charge purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion for armed forces members and dependents
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not consider any benefits, as defined in paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(3) of this section, received by an alien who, at the time of receipt, filing, or adjudication, is enlisted in the U.S. armed forces ... serving in active duty or in the Ready Reserve component ... or if received by such an individual's spouse or child ... in the public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipt of listed benefits by servicemembers (or their spouse/child) while serving does not count in public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Likely at any time to become a public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Likely at any time to become a public charge means likely at any time in the future to receive one or more public benefit as defined in paragraph (b) of this section based on the totality of the alien’s circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is prospective and based on an individualized, forward-looking totality-of-circumstances analysis rather than only past receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Alien's household (adult or married under 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien is 21 years of age or older, or under the age of 21 and married, the alien's household includes: (A) The alien; (B) The alien's spouse, if physically residing with the alien; (C) The alien's children physically residing with the alien; (D) Other children not physically residing for whom the alien provides or is required to provide at least 50% support; (E) Any other individuals to whom the alien provides or is required to provide at least 50% support or who are listed as dependents on the alien's federal income tax return; (F) Any individual who provides to the alien at least 50% of the alien’s financial support, or who lists the alien as a dependent on his or her federal income tax return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household composition for adults includes non-resident dependents and those who provide/receive 50%+ financial support; evidence such as child support orders, custody agreements, or tax returns may be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Alien's household (child under INA 101(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien is a child as defined in section 101(b)(1) of the Act, the alien’s household includes: the alien; the alien's children physically residing with the alien; other children for whom the alien provides 50%+ support; the alien's parents/legal guardians or other individuals providing 50%+ support; parents'/guardians' other children physically residing with the alien; parents'/guardians' other non-resident children for whom parents/guardians provide 50%+ support; and any other individuals to whom the parents/guardians provide or are required to provide at least 50% support or who are listed as dependents on parents' tax returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household for children is defined broadly to include parents/guardians and their household composition; support and tax dependency are key indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective determination principle — totality of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of an alien’s likelihood of becoming a public charge must be based on the totality of the alien’s circumstances by weighing all factors that make the alien more or less likely at any time in the future to become a public charge, as outlined in this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators must weigh multiple factors together; no single factor alone is necessarily determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Age
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering an alien’s age, DHS will consider whether the alien is between the age of 18 and the minimum “early retirement age” for Social Security ... and whether the alien’s age otherwise makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge, such as by impacting the alien’s ability to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Age may affect employability and future support needs; regulatory text reserves some subclauses for future specification ([Reserved]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Health (standard and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: DHS will consider whether the alien’s health makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge, including whether the alien has been diagnosed with a medical condition that is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with the alien’s ability to provide and care for him- or herself, to attend school, or to work upon admission or adjustment of status. Evidence: includes but is not limited to a report of an immigration medical examination performed by a civil surgeon or panel physician where required; or evidence of a medical condition likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with ability to provide care, attend school, or work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical examination reports and other medical evidence are relevant; lack of insurance and projected medical costs are considered elsewhere under assets/resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Family status
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: When considering an alien’s family status, DHS will consider the alien’s household size ... and whether the alien’s household size makes the alien more or less likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Household composition (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(d)) directly impacts ability to support dependents and is weighed in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Assets, resources, and financial status (standard and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: DHS will consider whether: (A) The alien’s household’s annual gross income is at least 125 percent of the most recent Federal Poverty Guidelines based on household size, or if under 125% FPG, whether total household assets and resources are at least 5 times the difference between household gross income and the FPG; (B) The alien has sufficient assets/resources to cover reasonably foreseeable medical costs related to qualifying medical conditions; (C) Whether the alien has any financial liabilities or past receipt of public benefits that make the alien more or less likely to become a public charge. Evidence: includes annual gross household income excluding public benefits; additional income from non-household individuals who reside with or provide continuing support; household cash assets (checking/savings statements covering 12 months prior); non-cash assets convertible to cash within 12 months (net real estate value, annuities, securities, retirement/education accounts, etc.); whether the alien has applied for/received public benefits on or after [insert date]; been certified/approved to receive benefits on or after [insert date]; applied for/received a fee waiver on or after [insert date]; credit history and score; and whether the alien has private health insurance or financial resources to pay foreseeable medical costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor contains the most extensive evidentiary list; USCIS considers both income and liquid/convertible assets, credit history, prior public benefit receipt, fee waiver usage, and health insurance/resources for foreseeable medical costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Education and skills (standard and evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: DHS will consider whether the alien has adequate education and skills to obtain or maintain employment sufficient to avoid becoming a public charge, if authorized for employment. Evidence: includes the alien’s history of employment; whether the alien has a high school degree (or equivalent) or higher education; whether the alien has occupational skills, certifications, or licenses; and whether the alien is proficient in English or other languages in addition to English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment history, formal education, certifications, and language proficiency are used to assess employability and are weighed in the totality-of-circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Prospective immigration status and expected period of admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: The immigration status that the alien seeks and the expected period of admission as it relates to the alien’s ability to financially support him- or herself during the duration of their stay, including: (A) Whether the alien is applying for adjustment of status or admission in a nonimmigrant or immigrant classification; and (B) If the alien is seeking admission as a nonimmigrant, the nonimmigrant classification and the anticipated period of temporary stay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term nonimmigrant stays or statuses that do not permit employment may weigh against the alien's ability to avoid public charge; [Reserved] subclauses indicate possible further specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum factor — Affidavit of Support (section 213A) standard and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard: A sufficient affidavit of support must meet the sponsorship and income requirements of section 213A of the Act and comply with 8 CFR 213a. Evidence: USCIS' consideration includes but is not limited to (A) The sponsor’s annual income, assets, and resources; (B) The sponsor's relationship to the applicant; and (C) The likelihood that the sponsor would actually provide the statutorily-required amount of financial support to the alien, and any other related considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an affidavit of support is required, the sponsor’s financial capacity and the strength/likelihood of support are considered as part of the alien's overall ability to avoid being a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed negative factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The following factors will generally weigh heavily in favor of a finding that an alien is likely to become a public charge: (i) The alien is not a full-time student and is authorized to work, but is unable to demonstrate current employment, recent employment history or no reasonable prospect of future employment; (ii) The alien is currently receiving or is currently certified or approved to receive one or more public benefit, as defined in 212.21(b); (iii) The alien has received one or more public benefit, as defined in 212.21(b), within the 36 months immediately preceding the alien’s application for a visa, admission, or adjustment of status; (iv) (A) The alien has been diagnosed with a medical condition that is likely to require extensive medical treatment or institutionalization or that will interfere with the alien’s ability to provide for him- or herself, attend school, or work; and (B) The alien is uninsured and has neither the prospect of obtaining private health insurance, or the financial resources to pay for reasonably foreseeable medical costs related to the medical condition; or (v) The alien had previously been found inadmissible or deportable on public charge grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of any one such factor is not necessarily determinative but will generally weigh heavily toward an adverse finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavily weighed positive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The following factors will generally weigh heavily in favor of a finding that an alien is not likely to become a public charge: (i) The alien's household has financial assets, resources, and support of at least 250
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text is truncated in the chunk; the rule identifies substantial household financial assets/resources/support as heavily weighed positive evidence that an alien is not likely to become a public charge. The mere presence of such circumstances is not alone determinative; USCIS weighs them in the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surety bonds — forms and posting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All surety bonds posted in immigration cases must be executed on the forms designated by DHS, a copy of which, and any rider attached thereto, must be furnished to the obligor. DHS is authorized to approve a bond, a formal agreement for the extension of liability of surety, a request for delivery of collateral security ... and a power of attorney executed on the form designated by DHS, if any. All other matters relating to bonds ... will be forwarded to the appropriate office for approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bonds and related documents must use DHS-designated forms; deviations or other matters may require higher-level approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond riders requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond rider must be prepared on the form(s) designated by DHS, and submitted with the bond. If a condition to be included in a bond is not on the original bond, a rider containing the condition must be executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any supplemental condition to a bond must be executed on DHS-designated rider forms and accompany the bond; procedural compliance is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bonds — cancellation, threshold, and breach rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Special rules for the cancellation of public charge bonds are described in 8 CFR 213.1. The threshold bond amount for public charge bonds is set forth in 8 CFR 213.1. Breach of public charge bonds is governed by 8 CFR 213.1. For other immigration bonds, a bond is breached when there has been a substantial violation of the stipulated conditions. A final determination that a bond has been breached creates a claim in favor of the United States which may not be released by the officer. DHS will determine whether a bond has been breached and will notify the obligor and inform of appeal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation, threshold amounts, and breach procedures for public charge bonds point to 8 CFR 213.1 for detailed rules; breaches produce enforceable claims for the United States and are appealable in accordance with the part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees — Public Charge Bond and Cancellation request
rubrics_metrics.description: (LLL) Public Charge Bond, Form I-945. $25; (MMM) Request for Cancellation of Public Charge Bond, Form I-356. $25
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule establishes a $25 fee for filing a Public Charge Bond (Form I-945) and $25 for filing a Request for Cancellation of Public Charge Bond (Form I-356).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection burden estimates (forms and hour/cost burdens)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule provides estimated respondent counts, estimated hour burden per response, total annual hour burdens, and total annual cost burdens for various USCIS forms (e.g., Form I-129 family of supplements, Form I-129CW, Form I-539 and Supplement A, biometrics processing, Form I-407), and states that changes required by the rule may revise information collections under the PRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These estimates support the PRA notice and invite comment on the burden/accuracy of methodology; see specific form entries in the rule for numeric estimates (e.g., Form I-129 total respondents 552,000, hour burden 2.84; total annual hour burden for collection 2,417,609 hours; estimated annual cost $132,368,220; etc.).
